A MoMA Exhibition Revisits Architecture’s Civic Purpose in Postcolonial West Africa
text_paragraph_1: La Pyramide, Abidjan, Côte d’Ivoire completed from 1968–⁠73 by Architect Rinaldo Olivieri (1931–⁠1998). Photography by François-Xavier Gbré, Courtesy of The Museum of Modern Art, New York.
text_paragraph_2: In 1958, addressing the first All-African People’s Conference, the Ghanaian prime minister and decolonization theorist Kwame Nkrumah proclaimed: “This mid-20th century is Africa’s. It is the decade of African independence.” He wasn’t kidding. Ghana’s liberation from Britain, a year prior, triggered a veritable cascade toward self-determination across the region. In 1960 alone, seventeen African countries declared their independence. Eighteen more followed suit the next year, and by the decade’s end, thirteen additional nations had attained sovereignty. Nkrumah’s pronouncement wasn’t just prescient; it contained the kernel of Pan-Africanism, the idea — a catalyst for the region’s freedom movements — that all people of African descent should strive in solidarity toward prosperity, a prospect that fueled a potent optimism for a unified African future. A taste of the moment’s unbridled hope is palpable in the opening gallery of the Museum of Modern Art’s latest showcase of an overlooked slice of global architecture. Architects of Liberation ( AoL ), co-curated by art historian Ikem Stanley Okoye and Martino Stierli , the museum’s Chief Curator of Architecture and Design, delves into the built Modernist legacies of seven western African countries: Benin, Cameroon, Côte d’Ivoire, Ghana, Nigeria, Senegal, and Togo, all former British or French colonies. The architectural deep dive spans projects from the late 1950s to the late 80s. The exhibition starts buoyantly: Upon entering, a tone-setting dark foyer conveys the period’s energy through archival footage projected onto two big walls. The fast-moving images show bustling street scenes and festivals; the novelty of rapid urban development and widespread jetliner service; workers and politicians, crowds and construction sites — in short, young societies brimming with busy potential. The introduction captures a special time in African history, a vibrant juncture in which art, literature, and music flourished in the wake of successive births of modern states. Heightening the anticipation of what’s to come, the room is filled with the sounds of “ Indépendance Cha Cha ,” a Congolese anthem, composed by Joseph Kabasele, that became the de facto soundtrack for independence fights throughout Sub-Saharan Africa. In a nearby vitrine, Nkrumah graces a 1953 cover of Time magazine, proof that excitement about the African promise also spread far beyond the continent.

text_paragraph_1: Ebola en RDC: quatre mois après le début de l’épidémie, le pic n’a toujours pas été atteint, selon Africa CDC En République démocratique du Congo (RDC), quatre mois après le début de l’épidémie d’Ebola, le pic n’a toujours pas été atteint. C’est ce qu’a annoncé l’agence sanitaire de l’Union africaine, Africa CDC, jeudi 17 septembre lors d’une conférence de presse. Une analyse qui contraste avec celle des autorités congolaises, qui avaient indiqué la semaine dernière que le pic avait été atteint à la mi-août. En RDC, le bilan s’élève aujourd’hui à 7 404 cas confirmés d’Ebola, dont 3 577 décès et 1 776 guérisons. Pour le docteur Wessam Mankoula, des progrès ont bien été enregistrés dans certaines zones de santé, mais ils ne concernent pas encore l’ensemble des zones affectées. « Quand on parle de pic, il faut comprendre qu’il peut y avoir plusieurs pics lors d’une épidémie, estime le responsable de la réponse aux situations d’urgence au sein d’Africa CDC. Il peut y avoir une augmentation des cas, que vous allez contrôler, puis la situation se stabilise, il y a même une légère baisse. Mais si vous ne maintenez pas ce contrôle sur la durée, la hausse peut repartir ». RFI
text_paragraph_2: Niger: cinq personnes déchues provisoirement de leur nationalité sur décret d’Abdourahamane Tiani Au Niger, cinq personnes ont été provisoirement déchues de leur nationalité, sur décret d’Abdourahamane Tiani, à la tete du CNSP au pouvoir. L’annonce a été faite jeudi soir sur la télévision d’État. En deux ans, plus d’une vingtaine de personnes – critiques du pouvoir en place et proches du président renversé Mohamed Bazoum – ont ainsi été déchues de leur nationalité nigérienne. Parmi les noms cités, celui d’Ouhoumoudou Mahamadou, ancien Premier ministre sous la présidence de Mohamed Bazoum. Figurent aussi sur la liste des personnes actives sur les réseaux sociaux, voix critiques du pouvoir militaire en place à Niamey et actuellement hors du sol nigérien. Selon le communiqué, ces cinq personnes sont notamment poursuivies pour diffusion de données de nature à troubler l’ordre public, intelligence avec des puissances étrangères, participation à une entreprise de démoralisation de l’armée et atteinte à la sûreté de l’État. Depuis la création par le pouvoir nigérien, en 2024, d’un fichier des personnes impliquées dans des actes terroristes ou portant atteinte aux intérêts de la nation, plus de 25 personnes ont été déchues de leur nationalité nigérienne. RFI
text_paragraph_3: Burkina: l’ex-président de la transition Yacouba Isaac Zida s’exprime dans la presse après six ans de silence L’ex-président de la transition, Yacouba Isaac Zida, qui a dirigé le Burkina Faso pendant 21 jours après la chute de Blaise Compaoré, prend la parole après six ans de silence. Dans un entretien accordé au journal en ligne « Courrier Confidentiel », l’ex-lieutenant-colonel qui s’était fait nommer général de division analyse la conduite des affaires par le régime du capitaine Ibrahim Traoré, dont il était l’un des premiers soutiens à sa prise de pouvoir en 2022, et ce n’est pas du goût des soutiens du régime en place. Sur le plan sécuritaire, Yacouba Isaac Zida salue la « montée en puissance des forces nationales ». Mais ne partage pas l’idée du régime burkinabé, qui s’inscrit dans une guerre de longue durée. « Il faut mobiliser simultanément les leviers politiques, sociaux et communautaires (…) renforcer le renseignement, la coopération et une diplomatie adaptée » pour venir à bout du terrorisme, estime-t-il. S’agissant de la présence russe au Sahel, il souligne que « la véritable souveraineté ne consiste pas à choisir de qui dépendre », mais à se donner les moyens de ne dépendre de personne. Concernant les cas d’enlèvements de civils ou de militaires, Yacouba Isaac Zida précise que « nul ne devrait être privé de sa liberté » en dehors des procédures légales. RFI

title: Trump Has Deported Thousands in Third Country Removals

text_paragraph_2: The Trump administration is spending tens of millions of dollars to fly people, shackled at times for over 50 hours , to “third countries” where they have no ties — even when they have won protection in U.S. immigration courts. text_paragraph_3: On the one hand, what the U.S. government is really paying for is propaganda: The goal is to terrify immigrants into abandoning their cases and “self-deporting.” But at the same time, this administration is keeping its agreements, flight plans, and any information on who it has deported where and why as closely-held secrets. text_paragraph_1: Alors qu'il assiste à un congrès scientifique, Seydou Drabo a un déclic : « Une interlocutrice m'a fait remarquer que nous, anthropologues de la santé reproductive, sommes des observateurs des décès maternels, qui ne mettons pas assez nos connaissances au service de l'action. Cela a beaucoup résonné en moi. » L’idée de rapprocher recherche et action ne le quitte pas. Quelques années plus tard, une première occasion de la concrétiser se présente avec TRI-MOM, qu’il rejoint par l’intermédiaire de Fatoumata Ouattara, anthropologue au LPED et mentor depuis ses débuts en anthropologie au Burkina Faso. Celle-ci le met en contact avec Sylvie Boyer, enseignante-chercheuse IRD en économie de la santé et coordinatrice de TRIMOM. Lancé en 2023, ce projet d'envergure vise à généraliser le dépistage du VIH, de la syphilis et de l'hépatite B chez les femmes enceintes, et à sécuriser leur accès aux traitements pour éviter toute transmission à l'enfant. Convaincu par l'aspect opérationnel de cette étude de recherche-action, il y intervient en tant que socio-anthropologue, sur le volet qualitatif.
text_paragraph_2: « Les stratégies mises en œuvre dans le cadre de TRIMOM ne reposent pas sur des documents théoriques, mais sur les expériences des personnes engagées dans le projet, bénéficiaires, professionnels de santé ou scientifiques », souligne Seydou Drabo. L'un de ces enseignements de terrain est l'importance fondamentale du volet social et communautaire dans la prise en charge des trois infections ciblées : toutes font l'objet de stigmatisations et d'incompréhensions quant à leur fonctionnement et aux traitements nécessaires. De plus, le VIH et l'hépatite B sont des maladies chroniques à vie, nécessitant un suivi médical adapté et soutenu. D'où l'importance du rôle des médiatrices dans le déploiement de TRIMOM.
text_paragraph_3: Si la présence de médiatrices paires était déjà instituée au Burkina Faso, c'est le déploiement de TRIMOM qui a introduit pour la première fois une médiation communautaire en Gambie, assurée par des professionnelles du Young Gambian Mum Fund (YGMF). Un dispositif précieux, dont la pérennité peut être mise à l’épreuve à la fin du projet, les médiatrices ayant été recrutées dans le cadre de TRI-MOM. Les besoins d’accompagnement restent pourtant présents au-delà du projet. Certaines situations requièrent un suivi dans la durée et les nouvelles grossesses exigent elles aussi un accompagnement sécurisé. D’où l’intérêt d’explorer des formes de médiation qui s’appuieraient davantage sur les femmes accompagnées par le projet, qui connaissent leur communauté et le parcours de soins, afin de renforcer la continuité de l’accompagnement au-delà du projet.

Tourism Month: Advancing South Africa’s economic growth through tourism
text_paragraph_1: By William Baloyi September marks the end of winter in South Africa, and as temperatures rise, our thoughts inevitably drift to a weekend getaway or year-end holiday plans. It is also Tourism Month, a period that invites us to celebrate the beauty, diversity and experiences that make our country a destination worth exploring. Our country boasts some of the most iconic experiences and adventures, many of which are often only a stone’s throw away. From the golden hues of a safari across the vast landscapes of the Kruger National Park to the gentle ocean breeze along the shores of Durban and Cape Town, South Africa offers a remarkable tapestry of experiences. Majestic mountains, winding coastlines, vibrant cities, tranquil retreats, and hidden gems tucked away across our provinces offer something to discover in every corner of the country.
text_paragraph_2: As the season changes, there is perhaps no better time to rediscover the beauty on our doorstep and experience, first-hand, the extraordinary destinations that make South Africa a world-class tourism destination. Yet South Africa’s appeal extends beyond its landscapes and leisure experiences. Our heritage is woven into the places we visit, the stories we tell and the people who have shaped our country. From Robben Island and the Apartheid Museum to the Cradle of Humankind, the battlefields of KwaZulu-Natal and the historic streets of Cape Town, our heritage sites offer more than places to visit; they provide windows into where we come from and how our shared history has shaped who we are today.
text_paragraph_3: They invite us not only to explore South Africa, but to understand it, to walk through its history, engage with its diverse cultures and appreciate the stories that have helped shape our national identity. This appreciation of our natural beauty, cultural heritage and diverse attractions also carries a deeper significance. Tourism is more than simply visiting new places or experiencing the richness of our country; it is an important contributor to livelihoods, local economies and national development. Every journey creates opportunities for accommodation providers, tour operators, restaurants, local artisans, guides and small businesses, allowing the benefits of tourism to reach communities across the country. In this way, choosing to explore South Africa is not only an investment in our own experiences, but also in the people, businesses and communities that make our tourism offering possible. This year’s Tourism Month is observed under the theme “Growing South Africa’s Tourism Sector in the Digital Era”. The theme calls on citizens, young innovators, tourism businesses and partners across the sector to harness digital platforms to expand access to tourism markets, improve the visibility of local destinations and create new opportunities for inclusive growth and job creation.

text_paragraph_2: An enclave is a geographic or institutional space in which the functions of the state have been substituted by private, communal, or hybrid provision, and which therefore performs at a standard the surrounding jurisdiction cannot match. Estates that generate their own electricity, ratepayer associations that repair their own roads, business improvement districts that fund their own policing, private schools and semi-private former Model C schools, medical schemes standing in for public hospitals, and firms that build their own water storage and their own logistics around a failing rail network are all enclaves in this sense.

By 31 March 2025 the Private Security Industry Regulatory Authority recorded 637 675 active security officers working for 17 146 active security businesses. The South African Police Service employs a little over 180 000 people, and that number includes administrative staff. text_paragraph_1: The relief is palpable, the expectations are immense: On 1 September 2026, Senegal and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) reached a staff-level agreement for a 36-month loan programme worth $2.2 billion. Having campaigned on a promise of transparency in the 2024 presidential elections, the government soon found itself facing an unexpectedly high level of debt.
text_paragraph_2: A report by the Court of Auditors revealed that between 2019 and 2024, the previous government led by President Macky Sall took on undisclosed loans worth 25 per cent of the country’s gross domestic product (GDP). At the end of 2024, public debt suddenly reached the equivalent of 132 per cent of GDP, triggering a downward spiral of poor financing conditions, a loss of confidence and political polarisation. The IMF subsequently froze its $1.8 billion programme in 2025. This put one of the new government’s key promises to the test: to reclaim Senegal’s economic and fiscal sovereignty. The current debt crisis shows just how limited the room for manoeuvre is for a country that remains dependent on international financing.
text_paragraph_3: The issue of how to deal with the debt burden is dividing the country. What was initially a technical problem turned into a political one, ultimately leading to a split within the governing PASTEF party, which has been in power since 2024. On 22 May 2026, Senegalese president Bassirou Diomaye Faye dismissed his prime minister and former mentor Ousmane Sonko. During the election campaign, the duo – who embodied the political change of 2024 – had emphasised national sovereignty through economic and fiscal independence. Sonko in particular repeatedly made it clear that debt restructuring would be tantamount to humiliation, thereby giving the impression that the country could break free from the existing structures and dependencies. Thus, PASTEF supporters claim on social media that, under Sonko, the party had raised almost 1.7 billion francs in just seven months — without IMF assistance.

Colonial legacies and economic development in Africa
text_paragraph_1: 'Colonial legacies' refer to the enduring impacts, structures, and influences – cultural, political, economic, and social – left behind by colonial powers in former colonies. These lasting legacies have shaped modern identities, governance, and inequalities, often perpetuating resource extraction, language imposition, and social stratification long after independence.
text_paragraph_2: Economic development involves the sustained process of improving a community’s economic well-being and quality of life through policies, programmes, and activities. Focusing on fostering growth, creating jobs, improving skills, and enhancing infrastructure to raise living standards ensures that development moves beyond mere income growth to structural economic improvements. Combining both aspects of colonial legacies and economic development introduces a crucial argument about determinism and agency, raising the question of whether governance is shaped by circumstances or whether states can act independently to shape their own lives.
text_paragraph_3: While colonialism created enduring institutional and economic constraints in Sub-Saharan Africa, the contrasting experiences of Botswana and Zimbabwe show that post-independence leadership and domestic institutions significantly shaped long-term development outcomes.

text_paragraph_1: 'Colonial legacies' refer to the enduring impacts, structures, and influences – cultural, political, economic, and social – left behind by colonial powers in former colonies. text_paragraph_2: Economic development involves the sustained process of improving a community’s economic well-being and quality of life through policies, programmes, and activities. Focusing on fostering growth, creating jobs, improving skills, and enhancing infrastructure to raise living standards ensures that development moves beyond mere income growth to structural economic improvements. Combining both aspects of colonial legacies and economic development introduces a crucial argument about determinism and agency, raising the question of whether governance is shaped by circumstances or whether states can act independently to shape their own lives.

text_paragraph_1: For years, phone makers have described on-device AI as if it were mostly a collection of features. A smarter photo editor appears here, a better voice assistant appears there, and the chip underneath is presented as a faster engine for doing the same familiar tasks.
text_paragraph_2: The Dimensity 9600 Pro suggests something larger is happening. MediaTek says the chip’s NPU 1090 can support on-device applications using models up to 30B parameters, while the wider platform adds a 34.5MB cache, LPDDR6 memory, UFS 5.0 storage and a new scheduling system built to coordinate compute, memory and power more intelligently across background workloads. The company also claims a 51% improvement in LLM prefill performance, 55% higher token generation per watt and 40% lower power consumption for always-on AI compared with the previous generation. MediaTek’s official announcement frames that package as the foundation for more capable agentic AI on smartphones
text_paragraph_3: That matters because 30B-class local models have until very recently been discussed mainly in the context of PCs and workstations. Memeburn’s recent look at what AI local models you can actually run on 16GB, 32GB, 64GB and 128GB treated the 30B to 35B class as a meaningful step up in capability, not as a toy tier for lightweight assistants.
